historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Amphetamine-type CNS stimulants

starting.description: Known oral and clinical effects of the Ephedra alkaloid ephedrine motivated an ephedrine-substitute program. Subsequently observed amphetamine-related wakefulness became a clue for stimulant clinical use; the historian also considers prior ephedrine experience a possible influence on narcolepsy testing.

inspiration.description: A naturally occurring ephedrine lead and its observed physiological and clinical effects guided the substitute search; subsequent amphetamine observations informed stimulant use.

steps.description: The Ephedra alkaloid ephedrine produced circulatory and bronchial effects in animal studies. Clinically useful oral ephedrine effects and constrained supply motivated a search for a substitute.
Alles prepared ephedrine-related candidates; amphetamine sulfate had oral and pressor activity in animals and produced wakefulness in his self-test.

Alles supplied amphetamine for narcolepsy trials; the historian identifies observed wakefulness and ephedrine experience as clues. The 1935 clinical authors explicitly cite awakening animals and insomnia in humans as reasons to explore stimulant use.

In a distinct pediatric behavioral application, Bradley reported observations during Benzedrine treatment in 1937 and suggested medically supervised use for behavior disorders; the historical diagnostic group is not assumed identical to modern ADHD.
After comparative observations showed stronger central activity of the dextro isomer, Prinzmetal and Alles investigated it clinically in conditions responsive to the racemate.

The later L-lysine-d-amphetamine prodrug conjugated the established active dextro drug to lysine to alter its delivery; the patent describes synthesis and preclinical comparison. An FDA review identifies its dimethanesulfonate salt as lisdexamfetamine dimesylate.

design.description: Alles prepared and tested ephedrine-related synthetic compounds, including phenylisopropylamine sulfate. Investigators resolved amphetamine into optical isomers and compared the dextro form clinically. Later, inventors conjugated active d-amphetamine to L-lysine in a prodrug intended to modify delivery and reduce abuse liability; the FDA identified its salt as lisdexamfetamine dimesylate and advised that labeling reflect high abuse liability.

circumstances.description: The ephedrine-substitute search and testing of the candidate were planned; whether its particular initial stimulant effects were unexpected is not established by this account.

limits: The evidence supports the common amphetamine lineage, separate narcolepsy and pediatric behavioral applications, a later dextro-isomer comparison and the lysine–d-amphetamine prodrug; it does not assert a separate founding for each later analogue.
Bradley's 1937 behavior-disorder population is not automatically equivalent to modern ADHD; his full report and subsequent research were not read.
The separate anorectic class is outside this assignment.
conflicts: Rasmussen cites Chen and Schmidt's volume 21, pp. 351–354 report as 1923; the publisher dates that same report March 1924.

The patent emphasizes reduced-abuse design objectives and favorable preclinical comparisons; an FDA reviewer later advised high-abuse-liability labeling for lisdexamfetamine on the basis of a wider body of evidence. The two sources differ in context and do not establish the product is abuse-proof.
gaps: The full 1935 and 1939 clinical reports and their results are inaccessible beyond publisher previews; Bradley's 1937 report is likewise accessible only as an indexed abstract.
Alles's archival notebooks and the later manuscript cited by Rasmussen have not been directly accessed.
Alles's separate 1939 primary isomer comparison, cited by S4, has not been read directly.
The precise initial circumstances of Bradley's clinical observation and the later evidentiary transition to present-day ADHD treatment were not established from the original reports read here.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Wakefulness and insomnia during self-testing and asthma treatment led toward narcolepsy; later child behavior observations supplied another clinical direction.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: Includes self-experimentation and treatment series; the Bradley report was accessible only at abstract level.
